MINIMUM WAGE (STARTING-OUT WAGE) AMENDMENT BILL
First Reading
Hon TONY RYALL (Minister of Health)  on behalf of the Minister of Labour : I
move, That the Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill be now read a first
time. I nominate the Transport and Industrial Re lations Committee to consider the bill.
At the appropriate time I will move that the Transport and Industrial Relations
Committee report to the House on the Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment
Bill by 28 February 2013.
Nothing can be more sapping for the spirit  of a young New Zealander than to be on
welfare at such an early part of their life.  Everything that Governments can do to assist
those people to get into mean ingful work is important, and that is why this Government
is bringing in this piece of legislation, in order to assi st those young people. What is
quite clear is that this is intended to assist three groups of people throu gh the starting
out wage. They are: 16 and 17-year-olds in their first 6 months of work with a new
employer; 18 and 19-year-olds who have been paid a benefit for 6 months or longer and
have not yet completed 6 months of conti nuous work with any em ployer; and 16 to 19-
year-olds in training in a recognised industr y training course invo lving at least 40
credits a year. The starting out wage is voluntary, and it must  be agreed to by both the
employer and the employee.
18 Oct 2012 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 6005
As I said, we want to help young New Zealanders get their foot on the first rung of
the job ladder, and we want to make sure th at they have an opport unity to get that job.
This was recognised by the previous Labour  Government, which introduced a proposal
when it was in Government that would see people paid the same amount as they will get
on this starting out wage, but it was called something else and it was limited roughly
only to about 3 months. We are extending this  to 6 months, and we are making it apply
across a wider group of these younger people. So there is nothing mystical or magical
about the starting out wage. There is nothing mystical about it, nothing magical about it,
and nothing mean about it, because it is the rate that Labour put in place when it was in
Government in 2008. But we want to make sure  that that starting ou t wage is there to
support young people who are new to the workfor ce, so that they can get into long-term
sustainable employment.
We want to give them an opportunity to ta ke advantage of the labour market to gain
the necessary skills and work experience to  assist them through their working lives.
Indeed, this is what Mrs Dyson and Mrs Fe nton said when they spoke in 2007-08 when
the previous Labour Government introduced its equivalent of this legislation. What they
said was that there was a good argument to  recognise that for many young people, the
first few months of their empl oyment were a training period,  when they were learning
skills, getting experience, and providing skills so that they could add value to businesses
in terms of their long-term sustainable employment. Labour  thought it was right that
young people be given that opportunity, and that  is what we are proposing in this
legislation—to give them their first foot on the rung of the job ladder. So this bill limits
the period for an employer who can use the starting out wage for a young person who
works for them to 6 months, unless they are training or supervising others, and after this
time the young person is entitled to be paid at the adult rate by that employer.
The starting out wage also addresses the issue for many young people who have been
on a benefit and who face difficulty re-enter ing or gaining a foothold on the workforce
ladder. What we know is that the longer someone stays on welfare, the harder it is to get
into work—

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: That’s right.

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: —and, as Dr Calder would say, th e worse it is for their health.
What we know is that the longer people are on welfare, the worse it is for their health.
In fact, Dame Carol Black would say that being on welfare is equivalent to smoking a
significant number of cigarettes every day. It  has the same impact on your health. If we
can provide every opportunity for young peopl e to get into wor k, it is good for their
future prospects, but also for their healt h. The starting out wage provides an incentive
for employers to take these young people on. Those who have been out of the workforce
for a while may lack skills and experience, a nd this provides an opportunity for them to
get what is necessary.
As the Minister of Labour said in her press statement, the Government recognises
there is also a need to provide more vo cational training opportunities for 16 to 19-year-
olds. It is important that th ese young people are able  to engage in tr aining for industry,
and employers so far have indicated that th ey are not using the minimum training wage.
So this bill changes the status quo by providing for young people between 16 and 19
employed under contracts of service that re quire them to undergo training to have a
minimum starting rate rather than the mini mum training wage. So we have reduced the
number of training credits from 60 to 40 for 16 to 19-year-olds to give them the
flexibility to choose a range of courses without having such a heavy load.
I think that the response to this has been really quite remarkable. Large numbers of
employers around the country have said that th is makes a lot of sense. I think there has
been a pretty muted response from the union movement, really. I think it knows that the
6006 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 18 Oct 2012
previous Government brought something in on this, at the same rate for a large number
of young people. We are extending that to a wider group. The rate is the same. After 6
months they move on to the minimum wage that  is currently legislated. But what is so
important here is that we give these young people a chance and an opportunity so that
when they go and apply for jobs, they are able to discuss their eligibility for this support
with the employer. The employer can take that  into consideration when they make their
employment decision.
But people must know that these young people are being supported by the Parliament
to get their foot on the first rung of the employmen t ladder. Just under 25,000 young
people have already benefited from subsid ised work placements and pre-employment
training. The Government’s plan is work ing. There are around about 60,000 more jobs
in the economy today than there were a little  while ago, and, despite  the uncertainty in
so many parts of the world, the latest GDP figures show that New Zealand grew by 1.6
percent in the last 6 months. That is very, very significant. Economic growth is forecast
to increase to 2 to 3 percen t, and that is what drives real jobs in the New Zealand
economy. Getting the private sector up and r unning creates the wealth and the jobs and
the economic growth that creates more jobs and economic growth for New Zealanders.
This Government has taken a number of important steps under the leadership and
auspices of the Minister of Labour, Kate  Wilkinson. The 90-day trial period for new
employees is deemed to create around about 13,000 new jobs. The lower company tax
rate is really competitive with Australia, at 28c. Hundreds of millions of dollars are
being put back into the economy through lower ACC levies. Hundreds of millions of
dollars are being saved by removing 170 unnecessary red-tape compliance measures.
We have got one of the lowest inflation ra tes we have had since 1999. Interest rates are
at their lowest level in 45 years. This Gove rnment is putting in place the platform that
provides the incentive and the encouragement fo r business to invest and grow jobs and
create wealth in New Zealand. The people who are benefiting from that investment will
be the young New Zealanders who will get in creased opportunities under this change
that is being provided by this Government. We promised to do it in the election. We
have got a mandate to do this. We have got a mandate from New Zealanders to do this
because it helps put the incentives in the right place to give businesses the confidence to
grow, to invest in their workforces, and to compete in the world economy.
I am very pleased to be able to move the first reading motion for this bill on behalf of
Minister Kate Wilkinson, who works tireles sly with our other Ministers to create
opportunities for New Zealanders, and th is is a big opportunity for young New
Zealanders to get their foot on the first r ung of the job ladder to independence and a
better life, which we would want for all of them.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: I rise on behalf of the Labour Party to strongly
oppose this bill, the Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill. In fact, it
could be called the “Minimum Wage (Sta rting-out and Starting-out Again, Again, and
Again) Amendment Bill. The Minister of Health is wrong when he compares this bill to
Labour’s previous policy and amendments to the Minimum Wage Act around young
workers. We had a one-off, 3-month, or 200-hours new entrants rate for a 16 or 17-year-
old. It was a one-off whereby in their very first job an employer could employ them on
80 percent of the adult minimum wage. What th is bill does, of course, is extend the
unfair, discriminatory practices of this Government when it comes to workers generally,
and it takes us back to last century. This is  a last-century piece of legislation. Not since
the last century have we had youth rates for 18 and 19-year-olds. They are old enough
to vote, old enough to go in the army a nd fight, old enough to get married, and old
enough to have families and have responsibilitie s. Yet here we are, saying that 18 and
18 Oct 2012 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 6007
19-year-olds under this bill will be worth only 80 percent of the adult wage—for the
first time since the last century.
What happened last century when we had minimum wages, youth rates, for 16 to 20-
year-olds? When Labour came into power in 2000 the youth rate was just $4.20 an hour
for a 19-year-old. For goodne ss’ sake! Did that fix the problem of youth
unemployment? No, it did not. We had some  of the highest youth unemployment we
have ever seen in this country. It is a ve ry, very old-fashioned, last-century idea—the
idea that this Government seems to have, th at if you cut wages, that if you compete on
cheap wages, then that somehow creates jo bs. We know, from years of experience of
trying that, that it does not work. We need to do better by the workers of New Zealand,
but also by our young people.
This bill will add to the disappointment of our young people that John Key’s
Government is letting them dow n. It is letting them down, and it is failing to give them
hope. Numbers of them are getting on the plane to Australia, numbers are already
saving up their airfare to Australia, because  they know that even if there is a youth
minimum wage in Australia, it is going to be higher than here. They need a Government
that will provide them with a future that provides decent, secure jobs, not the low wage,
any job is a good job, kind of approach that we have seen from the Minister of Labour,
from John Key, from Paula Bennett, and from  others. It is a very backwards-looking
policy, and it gives one message to young worker s. It says to them: “You’re not worth
much.” It says to them: “This Government does not believe in young people. It does not
like young people. In fact, we dislike you so mu ch we are going to give you a pay cut.
There is going to be a pay cut.” If you are 16 or 17, not only will you be on 80 percent
of the minimum wage—$10.80 an hour—once, for your first 6 months of employment,
but if you go to a new job, you are going to have to start all over again. That is why it is
called the “starting over and over and out” kind of bill.
Many 16 and 17-year-olds work part-time jobs, they work casual jobs, they work to
supplement their income while they study. Th ey do not actually have a permanent job
that goes for 6 months. So every 6 months or every time they start a new job, if they are
working in the holidays, back they go, down the snakes and ladders ladder, back down
to the youth minimum wage. They  feel like they ar e just getting to be treated like an
adult and respected for the work they do, a nd down the ladder th ey go, back to $10.80,
over and over and over again. It is even worse in some ways—in many ways, actually—
for young people who have been on a benefit. As I said before, 18 and 19-year-olds
have not been on a youth rate since the 1990s , and we know that made no difference.
But what the Government is planning to do under this bill and under its policy is to say
to 18 and 19-year-olds: “If you’ve been on a benefit for 6 months, you’re so
hopeless”—even though that benefit might be an invalids benefit or a sickness benefit—
“you’re going to get punished if you get a job, by being on a youth rate for 6 months.
You’re so hopeless you don’t dese rve to get paid an adult wage .” What we will have is
people going into the workforce who are 18 and 19, working alongside other 18 and 19-
year-olds who are getting the adult rate. That is going to cause mayhem in the
workplace. I think it is going to continue to cause real problems.
There are very deep flaws in the thinking of this Government around the process of
18 and 19-year-olds. They were raised in  question time today by me, but were not
particularly well answered by the substitute Mi nister of Labour, the Minister of Health.
First of all, how will employers know if an 18 or 19-year-old has been on a benefit for 6
months? How are they going to know? The Mi nister said that oh, they will have a
conversation. That just says to me that he  has no idea what it is  like for a young worker
going into a job interview a nd having a discussion, a so- called discussion, with an
employer about their job prospects. What it will mean, in my view, is that employers are
6008 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 18 Oct 2012
going to be led into a trap. Th ey are already telling older wo rkers that they do not want
them. I have had three cases of that in th e last week—three cases in the last week—
where older workers have been told: “No, we don’t need you, because we can get
younger workers on cheaper wages.” Employers are going to be led down the path of
believing that they can advertise and say they  want 18 and 19-year-olds, who have been
on a benefit, on a starting-out wage. It ma y be that Work and Income refers young
people, but I have deep concerns about the privacy around that and around the
discrimination that arises in the workplace—not only the discrimination for those young
people, who may have been on a sickness benefit or an invalids benefit or a young
parent payment, but also the privacy of th eir information. Why should that disclosure
have to happen? They should be judged on their merits. They should be judged on their
merits as to whether they are the best person for the job. If they are the best person for
the job, they should get paid at least the adult minimum wage.
The other question I asked today was about th e Minister’s claim in her Q and A that
she put out with her bill, that this is not compulsory. That is just simply rubbish. What
she said was that it is not compulsory; the wo rker will have to agree. If a worker is
somebody who has been on a benefit, goes alon g and applies for a job, is sent by Work
and Income, is offered a starting-out wage  of $10.80 an hour a nd says: “No, I can’t
afford that. I can’t live on that. I’m going to  have to turn that down.”, they will be
punished. They will be punished by having a sanction of a 13-week stand-down from
Work and Income, which is part of the w hole sanction approach to beneficiaries from
this Government. So saying that it is not compulsory is quite simply ridiculous. A
worker in that situation has no power to negotiate, to reach an  agreement with an
employer and say: “Actually, I think I’m worth a lot more than the starting-out wage.”,
when they know that if they turn it down they are going to have their benefit cut and
they are going to be punished by this Government, which does not like young people.
It is a very backwards-looki ng policy. The regulatory imp act statement freely admits
that the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment did not consult with external
groups such as the Council of Trade Unions  and Business New Zealand. It did not
bother. Treasury suggested that this could apply to other groups of workers, so we
might see in the future other vulnerable workers—we might see other groups of workers
like Māori and Pasifika, who have high unemp loyment—on a starting-out wage. How
disgraceful. Of course it is going to have an impact. We are trying to keep young people
at school. We are trying to keep  them in training. What this  does is discriminate against
those who choose to study and make a bit ex tra while they are st udying. It will impact
on their incomes and make it more difficult for them to study. This bill is a disgrace.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: The time is right for the
Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendmen t Bill now. It is the right time for our
economy. We have delivered the platform fo r economic growth in New Zealand, we
have the opportunity there fo r young people to get jobs, and it is time that we enabled
those young people to get on that first rung of the ladder of employment. This first step
is an opportunity for somebody to get a job, who feels that it is the appropriate thing. It
is the right time now to do this. The economy is in a situation where it is the right time,
and so we look forward to the bill progressing through this House.
I think the Opposition makes a lot of a ssumptions about the profile of our young
people and the training they undertake. Trai ning can be a lifelong thing that goes on
through one’s career, not just at one stage of somebody’s life. Somebody may take on a
job in the first instance, but it does not deny them the ability to get further training and
education later as they progress through their career.
18 Oct 2012 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 6009
This bill gives options for young people. It gives them options at a time when we
need those young people to get employment. It is a bill that will deliver a brighter future
for those young people, going forward. Thank you.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: I would like to say that it is great to have the
opportunity to speak on the Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill, but
this is a shocking piece of legi slation. It is a bill of failure , and of a failing Government
that has no ideas and does not care about young people in this c ountry. In a country
where the median household income has been  steadily going downwar ds for the last 3
years, where hundreds of thousands of people are struggling to make ends meet, where
poverty is afflicting our young in ever-greater numbers, where important sectors in the
economy are shrinking—sectors like manufac turing and the service sector—and are
letting workers go, what would you do? W ould you encourage new investment? Would
you support employers to invest in new technology and the skills for their workforce?
Would you support our young, especially our young who are hardest to reach, those
who are disaffected, disillusioned, disengaged, and now increasingly disappointed with
this Government? Would you help them to  get into training ? Well, not this
Government—not this Government. It has on ly one direction, and I am not talking
about the boy band either. It has only one direct ion, and it is cheaper and it is nastier. It
is cheaper and it is nastier, and the cheaper and the nastier, the better this Government
likes it.
This bill is about failure. It is a failure in  policies, a failure of ideas, and a failure of
leadership. It is about appealing to faili ng businesses, because the only businesses that
are interested in paying pocket money to  young people to do adul ts’ work are dumb
businesses, bad businesses, and grubby little bu sinesses that we need fewer of in this
country if we want a bright er future. This is not about  doing anything good for young
people. It is not about helping young people to get a start or get ahead. This is, pure and
simple, about exploitation. It is about taki ng advantage of people often in a desperate
and distressed state, and compelling them into low-quality, low- grade, and dead-end
work. It comes down to this: this G overnment—the members opposite—just do not
understand the labour market. They never ha ve; they never will. They have no qualms
about presiding over a gradual decline and reduction in the wages of working people.
The explanatory note of the bill says th at it “is aimed at influencing employers’
demand for young workers.” It will not influe nce demand for young workers, because it
cannot. What influences demand for wo rkers of any type —young, middle-aged, or
old—is whether there is work to do. Either there is work to do or there is not. If there is
work to do, an employer has a choice to make. They can decide  whether to do it
themselves, they can decide whether to get someone else to do it, or they can decide that
they just will not do it at all. Whether or not you get someone else to do it depends on
whether there is dollar to be made, or as ec onomists would say, that the margin of cost
of employing that unit of labour is less than the benefit or return to the business. That is
how the labour market works. That is what employment is about. The members opposite
all look down, because they do not understand this . It is too hard for them, and they do
not understand working people, which is why I do not care about them and why they
pass laws like this, which are unsympathetic and totally fail to understand the reality of
working people.
Now we get to the nub of the issue: it is about the price of labour. It is about the price
of labour, and this Government wants to reduce it.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: It’s about jobs.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: No, it is not about jobs, because jobs arise when there is work
to be done. Jobs happen when there is work to  be done. It is all very well for those like
the former police officer opposite who have en joyed the benefit of the largesse of the
6010 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 18 Oct 2012
taxpayer to talk about that, but the reality is that em ployment and job opportunities
happen when there is work to be done, and it reflects the state of the economy. And the
economy is rapidly going down the toilet, as it is under this Govern ment because it has
no ideas about stimulating it, giving employers a decent chance, and taking people on.
They do not understand that and th ey do not care about it, so they have put in measures
like this. It is not about crea ting work; it is about displaci ng good jobs that other people
have. If a dumb employer can see an oppor tunity to pay somebody $10.80 per hour for
work that they are presently paying $13 or what ever it is for, then they will go for the
$10.80. That is what bad employers do, and, sad to  say, we have some in this country; I
have met one or two. Fortunately, they are outnumbered by the good employers, the
ones who say that they would never indulge in this exploitative behaviour, they want a
high-quality workplace and high-quality workers, they want workers whom they can
invest in and they are willing to invest in them, and they see it as a relationship of
equals, not of one exploiting the other. That is the difference.
We know that this Government wants cheaper wages and lower quality, because the
Minister of Finance Bill English has boasted  about it. He boasted about it this year,
saying that a way to compete with Australia was to have lower wages, and everything
this Government does in employment legisl ation and industrial re lations is about going
down that path. Members opposite know that, they understand it, they are too
embarrassed to admit it, and they  are going to dre ss it up and say it is about creating
jobs, but this will not  create a single job, like  every other retrograde measure that they
have passed. It is lik e the silly 90-day “no rights” peri od that they passed. It has not
added a single job. It has not added a single job, it doe s not stimulate demand, it does
not help employers, and it just makes it harder for young people.
The worst thing, if it is possible to say that a bout different parts of this bill, is that if
you are a worker over 20 trying to get an apprenticeship, this bill will now drive down
the wages of apprentices. They are the very people who we need to be investing in. The
fitters and the sparkies, the builders, the car penters, and the instrumentation technicians
are who we need more of and who we are desp erate for. What does this bill do? It says
it is OK to cut their paltry wages, paltry as they are. That is the insidious, nasty thing
about this bill. Far from incentivising investment in young people, far from
incentivising skills acquisition and investme nt in a new skills base, this does the
opposite. It is nasty, it is evil, it  is tawdry, it is shameful, and it is embarrassing. It is
embarrassing to be standing in this House havi ng to debate a piece of legislation that is
so retrograde, that is so bad, and that comes from the 19 th century, at a time when we
thought we were making progress.
No good employer will be looking to this bill. No good employer will employ
anybody under this legislation. The differen ce between the National Party and the
Labour Party is that we will work with the good employers, the ones who are prepared
to invest in young people, the ones who are prepared to in vest in good jobs, well-paid
jobs, long-term, sustainable jobs, and decen t jobs that pay well,  not employers who
exploit young people. We will oppose this bill wi th every fibre in our collective bodies.
We have got 34 of them and we will be using all of them to  mount our case against this
nasty, insidious piece of legislation. It is just one of many that we know are coming
before this House from this tawdry, shabby, disaster of a Government.
We will oppose it, and we will be promoting an agenda of good jobs, of investment
in good jobs, and of working with those sensible, good employers who know what good
work looks like and who are prepared to inve st in people, who want to work with the
Government, work with the workforce, and wo rk with industry training organisations to
achieve just that. That is why we are opposed to  this. It is bad legislation. It is grotty
legislation from a grotty little Government.
18 Oct 2012 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 6011

items.speaker: HOLLY WALKER
items.text: I am sure it will come as no surprise to you, Mr
Deputy Speaker, or to anyone else in this H ouse that the Green Party is very proud to
stand opposed to this detestable legisla tion, the Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage)
Amendment Bill, to lower the minimum wage for young people in New Zealand. As the
party responsible for the legislation that  removed youth rates in 2008, we are rightly
proud in the Green Party of our track record of standing up in this Parliament against
discrimination and against driving down wage s to subsidise big business, and standing
up for young people and their right to a good life and a fair future, including fair
employment conditions and fair pay.
The reintroduction of youth rates for 18 and 19-year-o lds and the unjustified
extension of the training period for 16 and 17-year-old workers is a massive step
backwards. We have already heard from so me of our Labour colleagues some of the
compelling arguments against the reintroduc tion of youth rates. But why should we
listen to just the Opposition on this? Why should we rely only on the arguments from
this side of the House when there are pl enty of Government MPs who put the case
against youth rates incredibly well themselves when the House last considered this issue
2 years ago? I thought perhaps we should hear from one of them.
David Bennett, who spoke earlier in this de bate, has actually given one of the best
speeches against youth rates that I have ever seen. He said: “The fundamental
proposition this bill puts up is that we need to pay people less to get them into their first
job so that they can have an unskilled future. That is what this bill essentially will do to
New Zealanders. We see a different future for New Zealanders. We want those young
people to get into training and skills so th at they are not talking about getting the
lowest-paid job they possibly can, but instead are looking to  get the best-paid job they
possibly can. If we can achieve that, we can  make the dynamic change in our economic
base that will give New Zealand the growth potential we need.”

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Who says that?

items.speaker: HOLLY WALKER
items.text: I am still quoting—he is talking about the ACT Party, which
introduced the last legislation: “I think that is the fundame ntal point that the ACT Party
has not grasped. It is looking at things in a historical perspective. Well, the world has
moved on.” That was David Bennett in 2010. He is right; the world has moved on.
I want to quote another Government memb er, one for whom I have got a lot of
respect, actually. Dr Jackie Blue, in the same debate, said: “National has not seen any
evidence to show that young people are losing th eir jobs because of youth rates. We are
not convinced that this bill will reduce yout h unemployment. We should be focused on
growing the economy and providing opportun ities and jobs for young workers.” That
was Jackie Blue in 2010. That is why the Government members oppose youth rates. I
will leave it to them to expl ain, if they can without tyi ng themselves into rhetorical
knots, what has changed since they made those statements.
At the heart of the Green Party’s opposition to this legislation is the issue of
discrimination. I would imagine that there is  not one member of this House who would
today stand up and say that we  should have a lower minimum wage for women than we
do for men, in order to make it easier and help them find work. I would imagine that not
one member of this House would stand up t oday and say that we should have a lower
minimum wage for M āori than we do for non-M āori, to make it easier for them to get
into work. Some of them might think it, but I do not think there is one member in this
House who would get up and say it, becaus e it is ethically, legally, morally, and
politically repugnant to this House and to New Zealanders.
We used to hear those exact arguments. We have rehearsed them in this Parliament.
But thanks to some very brave, courageous, and passionate people who stood up and
argued for what was right, we have finished  those debates and we have moved on. Ours
6012 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 18 Oct 2012
is a society that understands and accepts and agrees that sexual and racial discrimination
in employment is not accepta ble. I thought that we had ta ken another step forward in
2008 when we abolished age discrimination in the workplace by removing youth rates.
So did David Bennett, obviously, when he to ld the ACT Party in 2010 that the world
had moved on. Apparently, some members of th e House are living in the past and they
want to take New Zealand backwards.
It is no longer acceptable to argue for sexist and racist employment policies, and it
should be equally unacceptable to discriminate against young workers. Let us remember
here that we are talking about young peopl e who are doing the same jobs, the same
work, as their older counterparts. These ar e people who are employed to do exactly the
same jobs as somebody else who is older than them but who will be paid 20 percent less
for doing that same job because of their age.
It has been illegal to pay men and women different rates for doing the same job since
1972, under the Equal Pay Act, and it shoul d remain illegal to pay young people
differently for doing exactly the same job as older people. Their work is worth the same.
They are equally valuable as employees. Real ly, as far as I am concerned, the argument
should go no further than that. We reject illegal discrimination in New Zealand. That
should be the end of the story. But, unfortunate ly, we have a Government that is pretty
relaxed about discrimination and is even willing to overturn the views of its own
members just a few short years ago to take us back down the path of youth rates, and it
is using the economy as an excuse.
Let us have a look at some of the econo mic arguments. I start, firstly, with the
regulatory impact statement prepared by the Department of Labour, which gives you a
flavour of just how much inte llectual rigour has gone into th e formation of this policy.
The officials note that the ministry has “not considered other options for achieving the
objectives of the proposed starting out wage package.” The reason that they did not look
at any other options is that it was a pre-el ection policy commitment, so “The analysis
has focused primarily on how to implement d ecisions that have already been signalled
by Government.” There is no analysis of  whether they are act ually a good idea, no
analysis of whether there might be bette r ways to address the problem of youth
unemployment. It was a preordained conclusion.
The regulatory impact statement also not es that “Consultation on the proposal has
been limited. The Ministry has not consulte d with external groups  such as the New
Zealand Council of Trade Unions and Busine ss New Zealand. The analysis has also
been constrained by the relatively short period of  time in which to undertake the
analysis.” So there you go. That  is the intellectual rigour. That is the economic analysis
behind this proposal. It was a preordained c onclusion with pretty much no basis. But
what we do know from the unr elenting and unpalatable rhet oric from the Government
side of the House is that the Government has an unrelenting focus on work, and it wants
to see young people off welfare and into work or training. We know this. We have heard
it time and time again.
The solution you would imagine, if you want ed to get people off welfare and into
training, would be to create jobs and training opportunities for young people. But that is
not what this Government has done. Oh no. It  has decided instead to give businesses a
massive subsidy in the form of absurdly lo w wages in an attempt to make young people
more attractive to employers. So how is it going to do that? Well, it is easy. It has made
young people incredibly cheap to employ. On  the poisonous starting wage of $10.80 an
hour it makes young people very cheap indeed to employ. They can employ them for 3
months and pay them $10.80. And then what are they going to do after that? Well, that
is easy too, because they have a 90-day trial period they can take advantage of—another
18 Oct 2012 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 6013
attack on young workers by this Government. So they can simply replace young people
with another cheap young person on $10.80 an hour.
As Kay Brereton from the Beneficiary Advocacy Federation of New Zealand has
pointed out, the result of th is is going to be that ta xpayers end up subsidising young
people’s low wages, and instead of creating new jobs, employers are going to have an
incentive to churn through young employees to keep the wage bills low. So they will
not be creating new jobs, in fact they w ill be creating the same job every 400 hours or
every 6 months, whichever comes first, over and over again.
As this Government so eloquently argued in 2010, the so lution to youth
unemployment is not to scapegoat young worker s. It is not to pay them less or to
discriminate against them and worsen their prospects. The solution is education, skills
training, and job creation. But what kind of incentive is it to pay young people,
including independent 18-year-olds and 19-year-olds, so little? Every young New
Zealander deserves a good lif e in a fair future, but you cannot have a good life on
$10.80 an hour. You just cannot, and you cannot  have a fair future when you are
discriminated against from the moment you enter paid work. That brighter future, which
this Government is so fond of referring to, is clearly not intended for young people.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: Andrew Little wanted to talk about failure.
Well, I want to tell the House about failure. Failure is seeing 9,000 young people end up
on the unemployment heap, when that party opposite decided it wanted to scrap youth
wages. We saw 9,000 young people not being able  to enter the job market, because of
the changes that that party over there made  to make it difficult—make it harder—for
young people to gain employment.
This bill, the Minimum Wage (Starting- out Wage) Amendment Bill, is all about
giving young people more opportunities. It is all about givi ng young people more
opportunities to get a foot in the job mark et. It is all about giving young people the
ability to get some experience to become mo re competitive in the job market, and to get
some jobs, because we know that l eaving young people languishing on the
unemployment heap is absolutely unacceptable.
We know that if young people are out of school , out of work, or out of training for
the majority of their teenage years, then th ere is a 90 percent chance that they are going
to end up as long-term welfare beneficiaries,  and being a long-term  welfare beneficiary
has a whole lot of other problems that are more difficult for them to overcome in life.
We know that getting them into training, or getting them into jobs, or keeping them
at school is an absolute priority. So this bill  is all about helping them in the job market.
This bill is all about giving them an opportunity to present themselves in front of
employers with a competitive edge, and giving them something so employers will
consider taking them on, because we know that if a 16-year-old and a 26-year-old front
up before an employer, obviously the employer is going to choose the candidate with
the greater experience. But if we give the employer an incentive, through a starting out
wage, to take a chance on the younger em ployee, to look at that younger employee and
say “Here is an option for employment.”, and to give them a chance, give them a “go”,
and give them the experience, then that young person gains that experience, and gains
the opportunity to get a foot in the job market.
We know that the Opposition actually has a very poor track record on jobs.
[Interruption] Andrew Little, you should listen to this, because your party has a very
poor track record. Your party saw 9,000 young people end up on the unemployment
heap. Your party opposed 13,000 jobs being cr eated through the 90-day trial, and we
know that the minimum wage changes that  the Labour Party wants would see 6,000
people end up on the unemployment heap too.
6014 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 18 Oct 2012
We are actually about creating more j obs. We are actually about giving New
Zealanders more opportunities—more opportuni ties. We have created over 50,000 jobs
in the last 2 years, and we have got anot her 150,000 jobs to be created in the next 4
years. The only thing we hear from the O pposition is more policies to make it more
difficult for employers and employees to meet together and create employment.
This bill deserves the recognition of the House. This bill deserves to be passed
through the House, because there are young people out there—young people out there—
who are crying out for jobs, and young people ou t there who are desperate to get a foot
in the job market. They know times are tough. They know that it is difficult out there for
employers. They know that the 90-day trial has helped them a lot, but  they need a little
bit of something else, and they know that this bill will help them further. This will help
young people get off the unemployment heap. Young people with a steady work history,
like all employees, are seen as less risky for employers to take on, but if they do not
have that work history, it is more difficult for them. This bill will enable them to get
more of a work history and more ability to get through the door.
The only options, the only alternatives we are hearing from the other side, Labour’s
solutions to the so-called cr isis out there, are more in flation and—the other solution—
printing money. They want to join up with the Green Party to print more money because
apparently they think that is going to create more jobs as well. They think taxing people,
taxing capital, will help employe rs create more jobs. They ar e absolutely crazy if they
think taxing capital is going to do that. Their other big so lution is to go back to the
1970s with industrial relations awards. That  was their policy at  the last election—
another way, another backwards step to make  it more difficult for employers to create
jobs; to make it more difficult for the economy to create jobs.
We are creating jobs in the economy. This will help young people. They can yell,
they can scream, they can moan about it, they can say whatever they like, but the reality
is that the statistics show that 9,000 young people left the employment market. This will
give them more of an opportuni ty to enter back in, get a foot on the ladder, get more
experience, and become long-term employees. This is a good piece of legislation. I look
forward to it being passed through its first read ing and hearing it through the select
committee. Thank you.

items.speaker: BRENDAN HORAN
items.text: I rise on behalf of Ne w Zealand First to speak
against this abominable piece of [ Interruption]—well, it is hard to say, really. You
know, sometimes it is hard to believe th at the MPs who prop up this National-led
Government live in the real world—particularly after listening to Jami-Lee Ross—
especially when it comes to the wages paid  to the ordinary working folk of New
Zealand. Since 2008 there has been a steady a ttack on the rights of workers, with
policies by this Government thinly disguised as “pro-jobs” or some other spin-doctored
euphemism. The minimum adult wage of $13.50 an hour is apparently, according to this
Government, hindering employment opportuniti es for the young. So a lower rate of
$10.80 an hour for teenagers starts next April.
The Government says this will create 2,000 new jobs over 2 years, but the problem is
that the latest household labour force survey  showed that 61,700 15 to 24-year-olds are
unemployed, and that is up from 41,100 4 years ago. So under the stewardship of
Messrs Key, English, and company, there ha s been a 50 percent increase in youth
unemployment, but they will create 2,000 new jobs over the next 2 years by reducing
pay rates. That is the sort  of twisted logic generated by fat cats, the unscrupulous, who
believe they can wallow in  their wealth off the b acks of hard-working young New
Zealanders. Nobody minds a successful individual enjoying the results of hard work and
ingenuity, but most New Zealanders believe in  the concept of a fair go. But not this
Government—oh, no. The minimum adult wage of $13.50 an hour amounts to about
18 Oct 2012 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 6015
$540 a week, and that is about $455 in the hand. This is a low wage, but many people
are still losing their jobs as under this G overnment the economy continues to spiral
downward. When National came into office, it ga ve tax cuts to the rich and it increased
GST. The Westpac boss, on his multimillion- dollar salary, got a tax cut of $5,000 a
week in the hand. We in New Zealand First do  not believe this is fair, but at least it
clearly shows which side this Government is on, and it is not on the side of those people
who are earning $13.50 an hour and it is cert ainly not on the side of those young people
who are soon to be earning $10.80 an hour. Fair ness aside, if we combine these cuts,
shall we say, with the job cuts such as  those in KiwiRail,  the Inland Revenue
Department, Solid Energy, and it goes on, it begs the question, how does this
Government make any money? How does this  Government make up for lost taxes?
When we then add a low-wage system into the mix, it becomes obvious that this
Government is creating a future with a serious  shortfall of taxable income because of a
low-wage mentality, declining birth rates, increasing longevi ty, and a complete lack of
fiscal prudence or responsibility.
The economic model that this Government s ubscribes to clearly is not working, does
not work, and will not work. This Minimu m Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment
Bill is a lamentable piece of le gislation and if the Government thinks this will in any
way create some sort of economic nirvana, or  contribute as a panacea-type cure for our
economically distraught country, then think again. In fact, it should wake up and slap
itself for even dreaming about it. It is pl unging this country into a low-wage economic
downward spiral.
You know, last night th is Government had the opportun ity to show an intelligent
democratic face to the people of New Zealand. It had the opportunity to take Winston
Peters’ member’s bill—the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Amending Primary
Function of Bank) Amendment Bill—which woul d have provided an essential tool to
help our country get out of its economic malaise, but, no, th at bar was too high for this
Government. Here was a tool where, correctly used, we could put a floor and a ceiling
on the New Zealand dollar, devalue by 15 to 20 percent, and reinvigorate the
manufacturing sector. That means getting b ack those 40,000 jobs th at this Government
has lost. We could weight our dollar to our ma jor trading partners to give it relativity,
and that would be relativity for our exporte rs. The floor and ceiling would give surety
and confidence, and we could export our way out of this mess.
There would be light at the end of the tunnel—you kn ow, the light that this
Government turned off with its narrow-minded course of austerity, the austerity that is
driving thousands of New Zealanders across the Ditch, looking for jobs in Australia,
and the type of austerity that is strang ling our economy here in New Zealand. This
Government demonstrated a complete lack of  comprehension of that bill last night,
because National members started waffling on —along with that turned-out prehistoric
alligator skin that sits over there somewh ere—about printing money, when the bill had
nothing to do with that. But such is the comprehension or lack thereof of this
Government when it comes to fiscal responsibility and the economy.
A lot of people have forgotten that  it was Winston Peters who saved—[ Interruption]
Jami-Lee Ross should be listening  to this because it is im portant that he understands
that when the Asian crisis hit, it was New Zealand that saved Asia. Winston Peters, on
behalf of New Zealand, guaranteed the Korean  currency pro rata w ith Australia and the
USA, and it saved Asia. A lot of people do not even acknowledge that. We should
perhaps look to history. Last night this Government turned its back on the opportunity.
It turned its back on the exporters of this country. It turned its back on the
manufacturers of New Zealand. It turned its back on democracy. A great bill could have
6016 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 18 Oct 2012
gone to the select committee, and we coul d have heard submissions, but, no, spray and
walk away.
We in New Zealand First realise that the G overnment’s role is not to be the solution
to all problems, but it should play an essential role in promoting economic growth, job
security, and fairness for all segments of societ y. Where in this bill is there reference to
apprenticeships or recognition of new skills an d competencies? This bill will be just a
recycled course for cheap labour. Perhaps it is  the cycleway that this Government has
been promising us, but it is a recycled way for cheap labour. Just as the New Zealand
public did not believe that larger classes w ould make their children smarter, they do not
believe that cutting wages will make the economic boat go faster. Thank you.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: As always, it is a pleasure to take over from
Brendan Horan, who has just finished speakin g—albeit that he di d have a bit of a
dampener on his own speech towards the end. In fact, you should always avoid raining
on your own parade.
I must say, having listened to the speeches , as I stand to speak in favour of the
Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill, that I have been disappointed to
hear the speeches from the other side. Talk  about dampening their own ardour. This bill
should be something that they support.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: What would they say in Glasgow?

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Why is it that is all we h ear from Andrew Little, a nice
person in every other way—I am left wonde ring whether it is just paid-up trade
unionists who warrant Labour’s support, rather th an job seekers. This is a bill to assist
young job seekers. I can well remember when I got my first job that I was delighted to
get a job. It was a pretty straightforward one—once a week helping a stallholder pack
up his stall. I was delighted to get going. This bill gets young people on the first rung on
the job ladder. This is a bill that addresse s real problems and creates real opportunities
for people who are not locked in the comfort of being paid-up members of a union, with
Andrew Little and the Labour Party to look after them.
This starting-out wage is  a great step forward from  the unpopular and unworkable
new-entrant wage brought in by Labour, the party whose current composition and
leadership could also be described as unpopular and unworkable, and it is demonstrating
it again in the way its member s speak about this bill. The new-entrant wage Labour
introduced had an abysmal uptake of 2 per cent amongst employers, and that is not good
enough.
That poor uptake and the 9,000 jobs for young people that were lost, as we heard
from Jami-Lee Ross, according to Department of Labour research, in 2008 after the
Labour Party’s move to abolish the youth wage, show Labour’s lack of confidence in
our young people and in the dignity of work. The people who go on to this starting-out
wage will be getting more money than they would get on the benefit. Why does Labour
not want them to get more money? I will  tell you why: because those members like
people on benefits. They like people on benefits. They like areas that are not doing
terribly well. It is most unfortunate. This starting-out wage will help inexperienced
workers get a foot on the job ladder, helpi ng them set themselves up for meaningful
employment. Everyone of that age on a benefit will be be tter off on the starting-out
wage.
We heard from Minister Ryall how it will be better for their health. That is a reality.
It is not made up. I listened to Holly Walker. I was disappointed that there is some sort
of virtue assumed in opposing this bill. It is  a very positive bill. It will help the very
people whom Ms Walker is espousing to help, without helping. She is  virtually saying
that you are better off being on the benefit, because then we can feel sorry for you.
18 Oct 2012 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 6017
The National Government is committed to creating an environment that encourages
economic growth and employment, both of wh ich this policy actively promotes. But it
is not only this bill that promotes a more prosperous and encouraging employment
environment; the starting-out wage should be seen as part of the wider package of
initiatives to help young people into work. These have already been mentioned by other
speakers on this side of the House. Let us talk about them a little bit more: the 90-day
trial period, creating more th an 13,000 jobs; increased flexib ility in the Holidays Act,
and goodness knows why that was opposed by Labour; the Government raising the
minimum wage every year with a balanced approach; and so it goes on.
Let me close by saying that we have heard much hyperbole and uniform negativity
from the Opposition around this bill. It is negativity that reminds me of something those
members seem to be forgetting: we, as sligh tly older people, should not be afraid of the
ambitious young; we should be encouraging them, and that is what this bill does. Thank
you.

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: It is disappointing. We are in the
middle of a crisis in this country. We need  change, and this bill, the Minimum Wage
(Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill, is as good as it gets from the members opposite.

items.speaker: This is all they can do
items.text: cut prices on wage s. All they have got in them are failed 20 th
century policies and no creative 21 st century solutions for the very real problems we
face as a nation.
What we have heard from the members opposite today can be described only as
astonishing. The last speaker, Mr Auchinvole, the member not  for the West Coast, told
us that this needs to be seen as part of a package that National has put together to create
jobs. Well, you have failed.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: You have failed—sorry, Mr Deputy Speaker, you certainly
have not failed. National has failed in its quest to create jobs. Let me tell you about your
record—let me tell National about its reco rd in Government. More than 50,000 more
people are not in work than when you took office. Every year 50,000 people leave this
country since you took office—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: —because you—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: —because National fails to—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order! You keep saying “you”.

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: —yes, I know—because National has failed to offer them
hope. This is something that the Governme nt has to own up to. There are currently
84,000 young people not in education, employment, or training. This is a failure by the
members opposite. This is 17,000 more than wh en National took office. This is not
something that members opposite can stand here  and tell us is pa rt of a successful
package to put young people to work, because si mply everything that has been tried to
date has failed. There are 17,000 more. In f act, 50.3 percent of Pasifika women aged
between 15 and 19 are curre ntly unemployed. That is  not something for any
Government to be proud of; that is something that any Government should give pause to
and reflect on what it is doing.
Then we had Jami-Lee Ross, who stood up and ranted that Andrew Little should take
responsibility for the 9,000 people who lost their job as a re sult of Labour getting rid of
the youth minimum wage. This is simply  wrong. The Department of Labour’s own
reports show that this is simply wrong. A report released says that by 2010 there was
absolutely no change in youth unemployment as a result of scrapping the youth wage.
6018 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 18 Oct 2012
Let us actually deal in some facts and not in some ideology. But you know what?
Even if this did work—even if it did wor k—this is a Government admitting failure that
this is all there is for New Zealand: the low road, a competitive advantage of low wages.
Well, Labour believes in so mething more for our country and for our people. We
believe in jobs, and we believe in high wages.  We believe in creating a real future for
people. We do not want to join the race to  the bottom that the National Government
seems to want to excel in. We were told we like people on benefits. Well, actually, what
we like is when people can work and there is a Government that is committed to
creating jobs for them, and that is exactly what a Labour Government will do. It is not
something we have seen this National Government in any way committed to.
I want to refer to some previous statem ents made in this House about the youth
minimum wage: “… we are not convinced it would reduce youth unemployment, plus it
would be a distraction from the really im portant work of improving productivity and
growing the economy in order to create long-term jobs, which will keep young people
in New Zealand.” Was it a member of Labour ? Was it a member of the Greens? No, it
was Paula Bennett in March 2010 in this Hous e. Then we had Paula Bennett say when
asked by Sir Roger Douglas whether she woul d be supporting his bill : “No, we will not
be supporting the bill, as we are not c onvinced it would reduce youth unemployment,
plus it would be a distraction from the re ally important work of improving productivity
and growing the economy in order to create long-term jobs, which will keep young
people in New Zealand.”
Well, have times not changed? Now Nationa l is not only supporting the race to the
bottom and a youth rate but giving up on increasing productivity, growing the economy,
and keeping people in New Z ealand. Actually, the only thing that National seems to
want to export are our people. It does not want  to do anything to help our industries that
will actually create these high-value jobs and keep people here. This bill that is before
us shows the lack of understanding that members opposite have of what a modern 21 st
century economy looks like. You speak to a ny high-value manufacturer in this country,
in an industry that will create high-paid jobs and keep our people here, and 15 percent is
around the usual level that wa ges make of its costs of  production—15 percent. So
tinkering around with wages is not the way to help these businesses stay in New
Zealand and succeed.
If you are content to have a low-wage economy and poorly pa id industries, then this
is the road that this Government is going down. This is not something that Labour is
content to be a part of. Labour has alternatives. We actually believe in giving our young
people the skills needed to take part in this high-value economy. Do you know what?
We would not let 80 percent of the $42 million budgeted to give young people the skills
and training necessary to take part in th e rebuild of Canterbury languish there unspent
while we do nothing to help our young people. What Labour would do is invest in our
young people, and it would get them into wo rk. It would not come up with micro
schemes that do very little to address the fundamental problem that we have: 84,000
young people who are not in education, employment, or training. The legislation that we
have before us today is going to do nothing to address that. It  is not something that is
going to fundamentally shift this.
Labour knows that in the 21 st century we have to do th ings differently. We cannot
have the disappointing failed policies of the pa st; we need to think creatively. That is
why Labour is backing things such as inst ead of paying the dole directly to young
people, using that as a subsidy to em ployers to get thos e young people into
apprenticeships, so that they get the skills and the training necessary for them to settle
here, live their lives here, and contribute to an economy that will be better for all New
Zealanders. But do we have any of that kind of thinking from members opposite? No.
18 Oct 2012 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 6019
All they can think is “Let’s make it cheap er.”—a bunch of salesmen who think the only
way to fix anything is to have a 50 percen t, cut-price sale and not actually look at
improving things. What we have is a Government opposite that has shown that it has no
ability to come up with  solutions when it comes to creat ing jobs in this economy. All it
has presided over is a growing dole queue and a growing queue to leave the country.
There are no solutions.
This is going to be another piece of legi slation that does nothing to address the
problem. It is another piece of legislation that is an attack on young people. It is
expecting people to live on an income that  is simply not liveable. I ask members
opposite whether they could live on $10.80. I as k members opposite whether, at the age
of 19—and they may have had a child—they co uld really have supported their family.
You put this together with National’s 90- day trial legislation—which members opposite
have told us, you know, has been so good—but where are the jobs? There are fewer of
them than when National took office. It is shedding jobs, not creating jobs.
This is a Government that has run out of ideas . It is a disappointment to all of us. It
has no ability to turn things round. All this Government can do is sit there and sneer and
not come up with ideas. This is a Governme nt that needs to go back and think about
how we really will back our young people in this country, because the Government
opposite is failing to do so.
SIMON O’CONNOR (National—T āmaki): In King Lear, the king said “Nothing
will come of nothing:”, and empty rhetoric brings about nothing. This Government is
committed to activities that support young people to get off the benefit and get into jobs.
You can hold and hide behind the empty rhetor ic of the ideology of this Opposition, or
you can get out there, like this Government is doing, and actually support young people.
This Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage ) Amendment Bill sits amongst a whole
panoply of other initiatives supporting our young people: this star ting-out wage, Youth
Service Corps, Limited Service Volunteers, Straight 2 Work programmes, and various
employment programmes. You need only to go  on to the Work and Income website to
see the wide range of initiatives that th is Government has to bring young people to
employment. And what is this Government  doing now? It is adding more—a starting-
out wage for up to 6 months to help young people move forward.
But what do we hear from the Opposition? We hear rhetoric—rhetoric of rights and
discrimination. The Opposition says it is a disc rimination. Well, we need to remind this
House that not every difference is a disc rimination. Boy, if it was, the Lobbying
Disclosure Bill that the Greens are putting forward would be a discrimination against
people who have a particular type of job. My God, I do not hear that being said.
This is a bill that is  nothing to do with discriminati on. This is a bill that is an
opportunity for young people to get jobs. It is a further opportunity on a whole
smorgasbord, a panoply, of activ ities that this National Go vernment is proudly putting
forward. We believe in the youth. We believe in their opportunity. Employers believe in
it. We are here to back them.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: It is sad on this eve of Labour weekend
that we should be in the House this af ternoon debating what I would describe as
National’s great leap backwards. This is what National believes constitutes an economic
growth strategy—

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I was just worried about the
honourable member when he leapt backwards that he might have hit his head on the
back—
6020 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 18 Oct 2012

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is not a matter of order of the House. Please
sit down.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: As I was saying, this is National’s great leap backwards, and it
was particularly galling and irritating to he ar Chris Auchinvole, the former member for
West Coast - Tasman, opining what a fantastic policy this is. This is the former member
for West Coast - Tasman. I challenge that  member to go and knock on the doors of the
families of the former Spring Creek miners. Two hundred - odd Spring Creek miners
recently lost their jobs because of this Government’s monetary policy. I challenge Chris
Auchinvole to go and knock on the doors of th ose families and explain to them that
driving down the minimum wage is an accep table way to manage this economy and
build opportunity. Go and knock on the doors of those families and tell them that
working for $10.80 an hour is good for them and good for their families. Do it, Mr
Auchinvole. Do it, and come back and report ba ck to this House, and tell us what those
miners said, because I would be very interested to hear what they said to you.
What a disappointment—what a disappointme nt—this Government has been to New
Zealanders. It came to office by saying that  it was going to reduce the current account
deficit. It was going to ma nage the economy back into gr owth. It was going to reduce
the number of people migrating to Australia.  It was going to reduce the wage gap with
Australia. It was going to build more jobs . And what have we seen? We have seen
defeat and failure on every si ngle one of those promises. This Government has taken
New Zealand backwards.
Nothing illustrates the absolute poverty of ideas that characterises this Government
more than its bringing this bill, the Mi nimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment
Bill, to the House. This is a party that onl y a few years ago declared that increasing the
take-home wages of New Zealanders was its top priority. It come s to the House this
afternoon with a bill to legi slate down the minimum wage, to deliberately cut the
amount of money that New Zealanders ta ke home in their pay packets. It is
unbelievable. Those members’ idea of stimul ating growth is taking away the workplace
rights and the livelihoods of New Zealanders. We saw it with the 90-day fire-at-will
bill. We saw it with this Government’s will ingness to trade away our employment law
and people’s rights at work to Warner Bros, and now we see it with a legislative cutting
of the minimum wage. Those members are bankrupt of ideas. They have got no idea.
They have given up on any attempt to grow this economy and grow the prosperity of
New Zealanders. A couple of days before  Labour weekend, on a day when it is
increasingly clear that one of our finest manufacturing companies is going to be sold
into foreign ownership, this Government has given up. This bill is the best it can offer
New Zealanders to grow the economy and improve the livelihoods of New Zealanders.
What kind of perverse logic is it when you legislate the cutting of wages for one of
the most vulnerable groups in our society?  As Andrew Little said in an earlier
contribution to this debate, jobs are create d when employers have  business confidence,
when they believe that there is a market for their products, when they have certainty,
and when there is work to be  done. There is no way, and it is not credible to suggest,
that cutting the minimum wage from $13.50 an hour to $10.80 an hour will create jobs.
This bill will not hurt just young people. By blowing a hole in the minimum wage,
what it will do is have a depr essing effect on the wages of all low-paid workers in New
Zealand. It is bad for young peopl e. It is discriminatory and unfair. It will contribute to
the growing sense of hopelessness that is driving thousands and thousands of our young
people across the Tasman.
What is worse—worse—is that it undermines  all the effort that has been put into
raising the productivity of New Zealand firms and New Zealand industry. We know that
New Zealand employers are addicted to low-paid labour. That is why they do not invest
18 Oct 2012 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 6021
in capital, plant, and tec hnology to drive innovation and productivity, and this bill
makes that situation worse. This country is hungry for political leadership that will raise
incomes and grow the productive economy. Th is bill does the opposite of that, and
Labour will fight it every step of the way.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: I feel a tad weary standing here this afternoon to talk to this
bill, the Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill. It is  another bill that
demonstrates a lack of understanding of the hardship in our communities, and it is based
on an economic vision that seems almost Dick ensian to me. This is another bill that
seems to be part of this Government’s drive towards a low-wage economy, this time
directly targeting young people.
My colleague Holly Walker, as well as David Bennett, Jackie Blue, and Paula
Bennett have all spoken so eloquently on the re al evils of this bill, so today I would
really like to just tell a st ory that I was told recently of a young woman who lives in
Hamilton, because I think it is quite inform ative, and I hope everyone in the House
listens.
This young woman is Stephanie. She is  making a living—or trying to make a
living—by cleaning. She earns what is soon to be the adult minimum wage of $13.50 an
hour. Like many other young people she is und eremployed, but she is working really
hard to stay off the dole. At present she works 25 hours a week, and to work these hours
she has to travel from site to site in the evenings to do her clea ning work. She has been
trying for a year to get more  hours of work or to find a second job, but, as everyone
knows, in this labour market  and without access to a com puter, when you are new to a
city that is really hard.
For 25 hours a week at $13.50 an hour she gets $337.50 before tax a week to pay her
bills. Out of this she has been able to pay the rent for her small flat, power, food, and a
prepay cellphone. There is little left over to save for emergencies like she faced earlier
this year. After a year of  cycling from site to s ite—a good green young woman—her
bike broke, and it was going to cost her $90 to  fix it. This meant that she had to walk
from site to site while she saved to fix it. How responsible  is this young woman? She is
amazing. But, you know, there are consequences of that—two pretty big negative ones.
One is that quite often at night while wa lking she would get harassed by men driving
past her, which is a pretty scary experience for a young woman in a new city. Secondly,
she wore big holes in her shoes, so big that it was not safe to wear those shoes to work,
and she knew that if she did she would get turned away from her job.
Does this remind you of Dickens, or not? Stephanie was forced to make a choice.
She had to get new shoes so that she could work, and this meant not paying for
something. I would like to as k everyone in this House wh at you would give up to pay
for those shoes. This is a young woman in work whose income, if this bill goes through,
will be significantly lower than that. Somebody who is having to give up food or paying
for her power to pay for shoes to get to her jo b—that is what we talking about with this
bill.
I think the question before this House should be: how can we  better support young
people to actually be able to live their poten tial and work, and be able to have a life as
well as that job? If low-wage work lifted people out of unemployment and into well-
paid jobs, hey, we would be fine with this, but the evidence shows that it does not. For
the member across the House to say that “They are better off than being on a benefit, so
really, hey, that’s great.”, is treating them  as if they are charity cases rather than
workers. It is saying that they should be gr ateful for a job and take whatever they are
given. That is offensive.
If this Government was serious about addressing youth unemployment, then there are
lots of things it could do. It could revers e the 2010 tax switch, which cost $2 billion in
6022 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 18 Oct 2012
just over 18 months. It could put this m oney into supporting small and medium sized
enterprises to take on young staff, create jobs, and it could support the member’s bill
that was drawn from the ballot today; a Labour member’s bill about committing to a
high-wage economy and supporting young people’s employment rights.

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: As this debate on the first reading of
the Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amen dment Bill draws to  a conclusion today
it has been interesting to sit here in the Chamber and listen to the stark contrast between
Government speakers and Opposition speakers in  terms of a glass half-full or a glass
half-empty type of approach. On this si de of the House we have been promoting
optimism, opportunity, hope, and collaborati on between young pe ople and employers,
and an opportunity to give them something they  want in terms of getting that first step
on the ladder of opportun ity that goes with being in em ployment. On this side of the
House we understand the virtue and the be nefit of work, of good, honest, decent work,
and we know how much our young people want to  be part of the employed and part of
the opportunity that comes from having a job and being on the ladder of employment. In
Coromandel I have young people who are welcoming this bill. They are saying “Bring it
on! Bring it on fast, because we want to have an opportunity to get into paid
employment.”
What Labour members are saying is that they  want to keep people on the dole. They
want to keep people on benefits. Christopher Auchinvole made that point so well during
his very fine presentation earlier in this debate. Labour members want to keep people on
taxpayer-funded benefits. They do not have any interest in getting people into work.
Young people want to work, and Labour does not understand the simple motivation that
work and opportunity bring. We on this side of the House support th is bill with vigour.
Earlier on in the debate we heard that  Labour was going to oppose the bill with
everything it had. In fact, what we have h eard throughout this deba te is a half-hearted,
empty rhetoric coming from Labour members. They have not had their hearts in it. They
have not got any fire in their belly. They have got no ideas, no passion, and no vigour.
In conclusion, let me just say that this is a good bill. I support it, and I am very happy
to commend it to the House.
A party vote was called for on the question, That the Minimum Wage (Starting-out
Wage) Amendment Bill be now read a first time.
Ayes 61
New Zealand National 59; ACT New Zealand 1; United Future 1.
Noes 59
New Zealand Labour 34; Green Part y 14; New Zealand First 8; M āori Party 2;
Mana 1.
Bill read a first time.
Bill referred to the Transport and Industrial Relations Committee.
Hon CHRIS TREMAIN (Minister of Internal Affairs)  on behalf of the Minister
of Labour: I move, That the Minimum Wage (Startin g-out Wage) Amendment Bill be
reported back to the House by 28 February 2013.
Motion agreed to.

Prisons, Private Management—Tabling of Contract 
CHARLES CHAUVEL (Labour) : I raise a point of or der, Mr Speaker. Under 
section 199I of the Corrections Act 2004, with in 12 days after a prison management 
contract is entered into the Minister must pr esent a copy of that contract to the House. 
According to news reports, Serco Group plc advised the London Stock Exchange 12 
sitting days ago of its entry into such an arrangement with the New Zealand Department 
of Corrections. I wondered whether I might ask the Minister of Corrections, through 
you, Mr Speaker, about her inten tions to table the arrangement  with the consortium of 
which Serco is a member, given the statutory requirement that I have cited. 
Mr SPEAKER: I am prepared to invite the Minister  to indicate a response to that if 
that is possible.

Department of Corrections has been working with the Clerk on the presentation of that, 
and I understand that it is imminent. 
CHARLES CHAUVEL (Labour) : I raise a point of orde r, Mr Speaker. May I ask

House. I believe that the member is raising a relevant issue. If the Minister does not

because it is required by the Corrections Act. Th at is, I think, as far as the matter can be 
taken right now.

QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Question No. 1 to Minister 
Hon NANAIA MAHUTA (Labour—Hauraki-Waikato) : I seek leave to hold this 
question over until the Minister of Education is present and available to answer it. 
Mr SPEAKER : Leave is sought for that course of action. Is there any objection?
